prompt:
A school needs to elect its president. The school has $121$ students, each of whom belongs to one of two tribes: Geometers or Algebraists. Two candidates are running for president: one Geometer and one Algebraist. The Geometers vote only for Geometers and the Algebraists only for Algebraists. There are more Algebraists than Geometers, but the Geometers are resourceful. They convince the school that the following two-step procedure is fairer:

(a) The school is divided into $11$ groups, with $11$ students in each group. Each group elects a representative for step 2.

(b) The $11$ elected representatives elect a president.

Not only do the Geometers manage to have this two-step procedure approved, they also volunteer to assign the students to groups for step 1. What is the minimum number of Geometers in the school that guarantees they can elect a Geometer as president? (In any stage of voting, the majority wins.)

solutions.title: Work backwards from the final vote
solutions.body:
**Step 2.** A Geometer becomes president exactly when at least $6$ of the $11$ representatives are Geometers.

**Step 1.** A group of $11$ elects a Geometer exactly when it contains at least $6$ Geometers.

**Enough.** With $36$ Geometers, put $6$ Geometers (and $5$ Algebraists) in each of $6$ groups, and fill the other $5$ groups with the remaining $85-30=55$ Algebraists. Six groups elect Geometers, and the Geometer wins $6$ to $5$.

**Necessary.** To win, the Geometers need $6$ groups with at least $6$ Geometers each, so at least $6\cdot 6=36$ Geometers. With $35$ or fewer, at most $5$ groups can have a Geometer majority, and the Algebraist wins.

**Answer: 36**

prompt:
Amelia's mother proposes a game. "Pick two of the shapes below," she says to Amelia. (The shapes are an equilateral triangle, a parallelogram, an isosceles trapezoid, a kite, and an ellipse. These shapes are drawn to scale.) Amelia's mother continues: "I will draw those two shapes on a sheet of paper, in whatever position and orientation I choose, without overlapping them. Then you draw a straight line that cuts both shapes, so that each shape is divided into two congruent halves."

Which two of the shapes should Amelia choose to guarantee that she can succeed? Given that choice of shapes, explain how Amelia can draw her line, what property of those shapes makes it possible for her to do so, and why this would not work with any other pair of these shapes.

solutions.title: Half-turn symmetry
solutions.body:
**The winning choice: the parallelogram and the ellipse.** Both shapes have a *center* $O$: a half-turn ($180^\circ$ rotation) about $O$ maps the shape onto itself. If a line passes through $O$, the half-turn about $O$ maps the line to itself and swaps the two sides of it. So it maps one half of the shape onto the other, and the two halves are congruent. So whatever positions her mother chooses, Amelia draws the line through the centers of the two shapes (the intersection of the parallelogram's diagonals and the center of the ellipse). It cuts each shape into two congruent halves.

**Why no other pair works.** Two congruent halves have equal areas, so a good line must split the area of each shape in half. For a shape with a center $O$, an area-halving line must pass through $O$: a line not through $O$ and its half-turn image are two different parallel lines, and the half of the shape on the side away from $O$ is strictly smaller than half.

The triangle, the trapezoid and the kite have only finitely many lines that cut them into congruent halves. For the equilateral triangle: a line not through a vertex cuts it into a triangle and a quadrilateral, which are not congruent. A line through a vertex gives two triangles of equal area only if it is the median, so the only good lines are the three axes of symmetry. Similarly, the isosceles trapezoid and the kite each have just one good line, their axis of symmetry.

So if Amelia picks at least one of these three shapes, her mother can place it so that none of its (finitely many) good lines is a good line of the other shape. If the other shape is the parallelogram or the ellipse, she makes sure that the axes miss its center. If the other shape is also one of the three, she makes sure that no axis of one coincides with an axis of the other, e.g. by tilting it slightly. Then no line works for both shapes.

**Answer: the parallelogram and the ellipse** (both have $180^\circ$ rotational symmetry, so the line through their two centers works).

prompt:
Sugar Station sells $44$ different kinds of candies, packaged one to a box. Each box is priced at a positive integer number of cents, and it costs \$1.51 to buy one of every kind. (There is no discount based on the number of candies in a purchase.) Unfortunately, Anna only has \$0.75.

(a) Show that Anna can buy at least $22$ boxes, each containing a different candy.

(b) Show that Anna can do even better, buying at least $25$ boxes, each containing a different candy.
answer: (a) Split the candies into two groups of $22$; one group costs at most $75$ cents. (b) The $25$ cheapest candies cost at most $75$ cents: look at the $19$th most expensive candy and split into cases on whether it costs at least $4$ cents.

solutions.title: Halves, then the 19th most expensive candy
solutions.body:
All prices are in cents; the total is $151$.

**(a)** Split the $44$ kinds into any two groups of $22$. Their costs add up to $151$, so they cannot both be $76$ or more. One group costs at most $75$ cents, and Anna buys that group.

**(b)** List the candies from most to least expensive, $p_1\ge p_2\ge\dots\ge p_{44}$, and look at $p_{19}$.

- If $p_{19}\ge 4$, then $p_1,\dots,p_{19}\ge 4$, so the $19$ most expensive candies cost at least $76$. The remaining $25$ candies cost at most $151-76=75$.
- If $p_{19}\le 3$, then each of $p_{20},\dots,p_{44}$ is at most $3$, so these $25$ candies cost at most $25\cdot 3=75$.

Either way, the $25$ cheapest candies cost at most $75$ cents, so Anna can buy $25$ different candies. ∎

prompt: Sasha wants to bake $6$ cookies in his $8$ inch $\times$ $8$ inch square baking sheet. With a cookie cutter, he cuts out from the dough six circular shapes, each exactly $3$ inches in diameter. Can he place these six dough shapes on the baking sheet without the shapes touching each other? If yes, show us how. If no, explain why not. (Assume that the dough does not expand during baking.)
answer: Yes. Put the centers at the points $(0,0),(5,0),\left(\tfrac52,\tfrac53\right),\left(0,\tfrac{10}3\right),\left(5,\tfrac{10}3\right),\left(\tfrac52,5\right)$ of the central $5\times5$ square; the closest centers are $\sqrt{325}/6\approx3.005>3$ apart.

solutions.title: Stagger the centers in the middle 5 by 5 square
solutions.body:
A cookie of radius $1.5$ fits on the sheet exactly when its center is at least $1.5$ from every edge. So the centers must lie in the middle $5\times5$ square. Two cookies do not touch exactly when their centers are more than $3$ apart.

Use coordinates on the middle square, $0\le x,y\le 5$. Divide it into halves in one direction and thirds in the other. This gives a grid of six $\tfrac52\times\tfrac53$ rectangles with grid points $x\in\{0,\tfrac52,5\}$, $y\in\{0,\tfrac53,\tfrac{10}3,5\}$. Put the centers at alternate grid points, like the black squares of a checkerboard:
$$(0,0),\ (5,0),\ \left(\tfrac52,\tfrac53\right),\ \left(0,\tfrac{10}3\right),\ \left(5,\tfrac{10}3\right),\ \left(\tfrac52,5\right).$$
Distances between centers:
- diagonal neighbours, e.g. $(0,0)$ and $\left(\tfrac52,\tfrac53\right)$: $\sqrt{\left(\tfrac52\right)^2+\left(\tfrac53\right)^2}=\sqrt{\tfrac{225+100}{36}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{325}}{6}\approx 3.005>3$ (because $325>324=18^2$);
- vertical neighbours, e.g. $(0,0)$ and $\left(0,\tfrac{10}3\right)$: $\tfrac{10}{3}>3$;
- all other pairs are even farther apart ($5$ or more horizontally, or $\tfrac{10}{3}$ vertically together with $\tfrac52$ horizontally).

So the six cookies fit and no two touch, although just barely.

**Answer: Yes** (with the arrangement above). ∎

prompt:
Let $S_n$ be the sum of the first $n$ prime numbers. For example,
$$S_5 = 2+3+5+7+11 = 28.$$
Does there exist an integer $k$ such that $S_{2023} < k^2 < S_{2024}$?

solutions.title: Squares as sums of odd numbers
solutions.body:
**Yes.** Let $p_n$ be the $n$-th prime, and let $k$ be the smallest integer with $k^2>S_{2023}$. Recall that $k^2=1+3+5+\dots+(2k-1)$.

**Claim: $2k-1\le p_{2023}$.** Compare $S_{2023}=2+3+5+\dots+p_{2023}$ with the sum $1+3+5+\dots+p_{2023}$ of *all* odd numbers up to $p_{2023}$. The second sum contains every odd prime that appears in $S_{2023}$, and also $1$ and $9$, which are not prime. So it is at least $S_{2023}-2+1+9>S_{2023}$:
$$S_{2023}<1+3+5+\dots+p_{2023}=\left(\frac{p_{2023}+1}{2}\right)^2.$$
By minimality of $k$, $k$ is at most the integer $\tfrac{p_{2023}+1}{2}$, i.e. $2k-1\le p_{2023}$.

**Finish.** Again by minimality, $(k-1)^2\le S_{2023}$. Therefore
$$k^2=(k-1)^2+(2k-1)\le S_{2023}+p_{2023}<S_{2023}+p_{2024}=S_{2024}.$$
Together with $k^2>S_{2023}$ this gives $S_{2023}<k^2<S_{2024}$. ∎

(Numerically, $S_{2023}=16{,}676{,}972$, $S_{2024}=16{,}694{,}571$, and $k=4084$, $k^2=16{,}679{,}056$.)

solutions.title: Contradiction
solutions.body:
Suppose no square lies strictly between $S_{2023}$ and $S_{2024}$. Let $r=\lfloor\sqrt{S_{2023}}\rfloor$, so $r^2\le S_{2023}<(r+1)^2$. By assumption $(r+1)^2$ is not less than $S_{2024}$, so
$$r^2\le S_{2023}<S_{2024}\le (r+1)^2.$$
Hence $p_{2024}=S_{2024}-S_{2023}\le 2r+1$. So every prime $p_1,\dots,p_{2023}$ is less than $2r+1$, and every odd one among them is at most $2r-1$. Then $S_{2023}$ is at most $2$ plus the odd numbers $3,5,\dots,2r-1$, leaving out $9$ (here $2r-1\ge9$ because $p_{2024}>9$):
$$S_{2023}\le \bigl(1+3+\dots+(2r-1)\bigr)-1-9+2=r^2-8<r^2.$$
This contradicts $r^2\le S_{2023}$. ∎

prompt:
Let $S_n$ be the sum of the first $n$ prime numbers. For example,
$$S_5 = 2+3+5+7+11 = 28.$$
Does there exist an integer $k$ such that $S_{2023} < k^2 < S_{2024}$?

Find all polynomials $f$ that satisfy the equation
$$\frac{f(3x)}{f(x)} = \frac{729(x-3)}{x-243}$$
for infinitely many real values of $x$.

solutions.title: Turn it into a polynomial identity
solutions.body:
**Identity.** The polynomial $g(x)=(x-243)f(3x)-729(x-3)f(x)$ vanishes at the infinitely many $x$ in question, so $g$ is the zero polynomial:
$$(x-243)\,f(3x)=729(x-3)\,f(x)\quad\text{for all }x.\tag{1}$$
Conversely, if $f\ne0$ satisfies (1), the original equation holds for every $x$ with $f(x)\ne0$ and $x\ne243$, which is all but finitely many $x$. ($f\equiv0$ is excluded because the left side would be undefined.)

**Roots.** Substitute into (1):
- $x=3$: $-240f(9)=0$, so $f(9)=0$;
- $x=9$: $-234f(27)=729\cdot6\,f(9)=0$, so $f(27)=0$;
- $x=27$: $-216f(81)=0$, so $f(81)=0$;
- $x=81$: $-162f(243)=0$, so $f(243)=0$.

So $f(x)=(x-9)(x-27)(x-81)(x-243)\,p(x)$ for a polynomial $p$. Since
$$(3x-9)(3x-27)(3x-81)(3x-243)=81(x-3)(x-9)(x-27)(x-81),$$
(1) becomes
$$81(x-243)(x-3)(x-9)(x-27)(x-81)\,p(3x)=729(x-3)(x-9)(x-27)(x-81)(x-243)\,p(x),$$
i.e. $p(3x)=9p(x)$.

**Solve for $p$.** Write $p(x)=\sum c_kx^k$. Comparing coefficients gives $3^kc_k=9c_k$, so $c_k=0$ unless $k=2$. Thus $p(x)=ax^2$, and
$$f(x)=a\,x^2(x-9)(x-27)(x-81)(x-243),\qquad a\ne0.$$

**Check.** $\dfrac{f(3x)}{f(x)}=\dfrac{9x^2\cdot81(x-3)(x-9)(x-27)(x-81)}{x^2(x-9)(x-27)(x-81)(x-243)}=\dfrac{729(x-3)}{x-243}$ wherever $f(x)\ne0$. ✓ ∎

solutions.title: Track the multiset of roots
solutions.body:
From (1), the two sides have the same roots with multiplicity. If $Z$ is the multiset of roots of $f$, the roots of $f(3x)$ are $\tfrac13Z$. So $\{243\}\cup\tfrac13Z=\{3\}\cup Z$, or after multiplying by $3$, $\{729\}\cup Z=\{9\}\cup 3Z$. The $9$ on the right must appear on the left, so $9\in Z$. Then $27\in 3Z$ appears on the right, so $27\in Z$ (as $27\ne729$); in the same way $81\in Z$ and then $243\in Z$. Write $Z=\{9,27,81,243\}\cup Y$. Then
$$\{9,27,81,243,729\}\cup Y=\{9,27,81,243,729\}\cup 3Y,$$
so $Y=3Y$ as multisets. A finite multiset of complex numbers that is unchanged when multiplied by $3$ can only contain $0$: a nonzero element of largest absolute value $m$ would give $3m$ in $3Y$, which is too large. So $f(x)=a x^k(x-9)(x-27)(x-81)(x-243)$. Comparing the leading coefficients in (1) gives $3^{k+4}=729=3^6$, so $k=2$.

**Answer:** $f(x)=a\,x^2(x-9)(x-27)(x-81)(x-243)$, $a\ne 0$. ∎

prompt:
An underground burrow consists of an infinite sequence of rooms labeled by the integers $(\dots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots)$. Initially, some of the rooms are occupied by one or more rabbits. Each rabbit wants to be alone. Thus, if there are two or more rabbits in the same room (say, room $m$), half the rabbits (rounding down) will flee to room $m-1$, and half (also rounding down) to room $m+1$. Once per minute, this happens simultaneously in all rooms that have two or more rabbits. For example, if initially all rooms are empty except for $5$ rabbits in room #12 and $2$ rabbits in room #13, then after one minute, rooms #11–#14 will contain $2$, $2$, $2$, and $1$ rabbits, respectively, and all other rooms will be empty.

Now suppose that initially there are $k+1$ rabbits in room $k$ for each $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots, 9, 10$, and all other rooms are empty.

(a) Show that eventually the rabbits will stop moving.

(b) Determine which rooms will be occupied when this occurs.
answer: (a) The rabbits stay in a bounded set of rooms, while the sum of the squares of their room numbers grows at every move. (b) Rooms $-26$ through $40$, except room $29$ (one rabbit in each).

solutions.title: Invariants, then a gap lemma by strong induction
solutions.body:
There are $1+2+\dots+11=66$ rabbits. When a room $m$ with $v\ge2$ rabbits discharges, $\lfloor v/2\rfloor$ *pairs* of rabbits move, each pair going from $m,m$ to $m-1,m+1$. Since $(m-1)+(m+1)=2m$, the **sum of all room numbers is invariant**. Initially it is $\sum_{k=0}^{10}k(k+1)=440$. Since $(m-1)^2+(m+1)^2=2m^2+2$, the **sum of squares of room numbers increases by $2$ for every pair that moves**.

Call a room *interior* at a given time if it lies between the leftmost and the rightmost occupied rooms, inclusive. The leftmost occupied room can only move left, by one room per minute, and the new leftmost room is occupied; similarly on the right. So the interior is an interval that only grows. Every room that is ever interior is occupied at some moment: at time $0$, or at the moment it joins the interval.

**Lemma 1. Two adjacent interior rooms are never both empty.** It is true at the start (rooms $0$–$10$ are all occupied). Suppose it first fails at time $s+1$, with interior rooms $A$, $A+1$ both empty. Both rooms were already interior at time $s$, since the interval grows by at most one room per side and the new end rooms are occupied. So by minimality, one of them, say $A$, was occupied at time $s$. A room keeps a rabbit unless it discharges, so $A$ discharged at time $s$ and sent at least one rabbit into $A+1$, which is then occupied at time $s+1$. Contradiction. (The case where $A+1$ was occupied is symmetric.)

**(a) The process stops.** By Lemma 1, the $66$ rabbits never leave gaps of $2$ or more empty rooms inside the interval, so the interval has length at most $2\cdot66$. If its left end is $L$, every rabbit is in $[L,L+132]$, so $66L\le 440\le 66(L+132)$. So $L$ is bounded, and all rabbits always stay in a fixed bounded set of rooms. Then the sum of squares is bounded. But it increases by at least $2$ every minute in which anything moves, so the rabbits stop after finitely many minutes.

**Lemma 2. For every $n\ge2$, at all times, any $n$ consecutive interior rooms contain at least $n-1$ rabbits.** We use strong induction on $n$; $n=2$ is Lemma 1. Assume the statement for all lengths $2,\dots,n$ (at all times), and suppose that at some time $\tau$ a window $W=\{k,\dots,k+n\}$ of $n+1$ interior rooms contains at most $n-1$ rabbits.

*Step 1: at time $\tau$, $W$ looks like $0,1,1,\dots,1,0$.* The window $\{k,\dots,k+n-1\}$ has at least $n-1$ rabbits, so room $k+n$ is empty and $W$ has exactly $n-1$ rabbits. Symmetrically, room $k$ is empty. If some middle room $k+j$ ($1\le j\le n-1$) were empty, the windows $\{k,\dots,k+j\}$ and $\{k+j,\dots,k+n\}$ (lengths between $2$ and $n$) would hold at least $j$ and $n-j$ rabbits. All of these lie in rooms other than $k,k+j,k+n$, so $W$ would hold at least $n$ rabbits, a contradiction. So the $n-1$ middle rooms hold $n-1$ rabbits, none empty, so one each.

*Step 2: go back in time.* Rooms $k$ and $k+n$ were occupied at some earlier moments. Say room $k$ was occupied more recently (or equally recently), and let $t<\tau$ be the last time it was occupied. Then from time $t+1$ to $\tau$, rooms $k$ and $k+n$ are both empty. Rabbits can only enter or leave $W$ through its end rooms, so the count in $W$ is the same at time $t+1$ as at $\tau$, namely at most $n-1$. Both end rooms were occupied by time $t$, so $W$ is interior at times $t$ and $t+1$. By Step 1, at time $t+1$, $W$ is $0,1,\dots,1,0$ and its middle $M=\{k+1,\dots,k+n-1\}$ holds $n-1$ rabbits.

Room $k$ went from occupied to empty, so at time $t$ it discharged and sent at least one rabbit into $k+1\in M$. No rabbit moved from $M$ into $k$ or $k+n$ at time $t$, since those rooms are empty at time $t+1$.
- If room $k+n$ also discharged at time $t$, it sent at least one rabbit into $M$. So $M$ held at most $n-3$ rabbits at time $t$. For $n=2$ this is impossible. For $n\ge3$, $M$ is $n-1$ consecutive interior rooms with at most $n-3$ rabbits, which contradicts the hypothesis for length $n-1$.
- Otherwise room $k+n$ was empty at time $t$ (an occupied room that does not discharge stays occupied). Then $M$ held at most $n-2$ rabbits at time $t$, and the $n$ rooms $\{k+1,\dots,k+n\}$ held at most $n-2$, which contradicts the hypothesis for length $n$.

This proves Lemma 2.

**(b) The final position.** When the rabbits stop, every room has $0$ or $1$ rabbits. By Lemma 2 applied to the whole interval, at most one interior room is empty, and the end rooms are occupied. So the $66$ rabbits fill either $66$ consecutive rooms, or $67$ consecutive rooms minus one inner room. The sum of the room numbers is $440$.

- $66$ rooms $m,\dots,m+65$: the sum is $66m+2145=440$, so $m=-\tfrac{1705}{66}$, not an integer. Impossible.
- $67$ rooms $m,\dots,m+66$ minus room $e$, with $m<e<m+66$: $67m+2211-e=440$, so $e=67m+1771$. The condition $m<e<m+66$ gives $-\tfrac{1771}{66}<m<-\tfrac{1705}{66}$, i.e. $-26.8<m<-25.8$, so $m=-26$ and $e=29$.

**Answer:** (a) the rabbits stop; (b) the occupied rooms are $-26,-25,\dots,40$ except room $29$, with one rabbit in each. ∎
